title: Perioperative Nursing: Preoperative Verification, Intraoperative Safety & Postanesthesia Rescue
html:
Perioperative nursing connects the decision for surgery with safe recovery. The RN creates continuity across preoperative preparation, the procedure area, postanesthesia care, and discharge. Priorities are correct person–procedure–site verification, informed participation, infection prevention, airway and hemodynamic rescue, protection from positioning and equipment injury, and early recognition of postoperative complications. Exact fasting, medication, antimicrobial, skin-preparation, transfer, and discharge requirements follow the procedure, anesthesia plan, current orders, and facility policy.

Learning goals

  • Complete a client-centered preoperative assessment and resolve discrepancies before transport or sedation.
  • Distinguish the proceduralist’s consent responsibility from the nurse’s role in verification, witnessing, advocacy, and escalation.
  • Apply preprocedure verification, site marking, time-out, specimen, count, positioning, and fire-safety principles.
  • Prioritize airway, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, pain, temperature, nausea, and surgical-site findings in PACU.
  • Recognize malignant hyperthermia, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, respiratory depression, infection, and wound disruption.
  • Prepare clients for recovery using individualized teaching, teach-back, and safe discharge criteria.

Begin with the operation and the person

Confirm the planned procedure, indication, laterality or level, schedule, surgeon or proceduralist, anesthesia plan, expected disposition, and whether required equipment, implants, imaging, laboratory results, and blood products are available. Then assess the person: baseline airway and respiratory status, cardiac and neurologic findings, functional capacity, pain, skin, infection symptoms, nutrition, hydration, elimination, pregnancy possibility when relevant, glucose, kidney and liver function, bleeding and clotting risks, substance use, sleep apnea, prior anesthesia or surgical problems, and ability to recover safely.

Reconcile every prescription, OTC product, supplement, herb, patch, inhaler, injection, anticoagulant, antiplatelet, diabetes medicine, steroid, opioid, and substance exposure. Record the last dose and follow procedure-specific instructions for continuation or withholding. The RN does not independently invent fasting or medication-stop rules; a missing or conflicting instruction is clarified before the procedure.

Allergies and previous anesthesia matter

Ask about the exact reaction to medications, latex, adhesives, antiseptics, contrast, foods relevant to products, and prior transfusions. Ask the client and biologic relatives about unexpected high fever, severe muscle rigidity, ICU admission, cardiac arrest, or death during anesthesia because this history may suggest malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility. Communicate risks visibly through approved alerts and the handoff.

Assess loose or damaged teeth, dentures, hearing devices, glasses, contacts, mobility aids, implanted devices, jewelry or piercings, and skin near the operative site. Remove or retain items only according to the clinical plan and policy; protect communication and mobility until they are no longer safe to maintain.

Consent is a process, not a signature

The authorized proceduralist explains the procedure, material risks and expected benefits, alternatives, and consequences of refusing, and answers procedure-specific questions. The client must have decision-making capacity and act voluntarily before sedating medication. The nurse verifies that the signed consent matches the scheduled procedure, witnesses the signature when policy assigns that role, assesses understanding and voluntariness, and advocates for clarification.

If the client says, “I do not understand,” changes the description, appears coerced, or wants to withdraw consent, stop preparation that would remove choice and notify the proceduralist. Never reassure beyond the RN’s knowledge or obtain a signature merely to keep the schedule moving. Emergency exceptions and surrogate decisions follow law, policy, and the clinical situation.

A signed form does not resolve confusion
If the client’s understanding, identity, procedure, site, or consent does not match, pause and resolve the discrepancy before sedation or incision.

Preprocedure verification prevents wrong care

Use two approved identifiers and compare the schedule, consent, history and physical, anesthesia assessment, diagnostic results, implant or equipment needs, blood availability, and procedure plan. Involve the client whenever possible. The procedural site is marked by the responsible qualified person according to policy and remains visible after preparation and draping. Never mark by guessing or use an adhesive marker as the sole method.

Immediately before incision or the invasive portion begins, the active team conducts a standardized time-out with work paused and verbal participation. At minimum, confirm the correct client, site, and procedure; the local checklist may also verify allergies, antibiotics, positioning, implants, imaging, blood-loss concerns, specimens, and equipment. Any team member can voice a concern, and the procedure does not proceed until it is resolved.

Prepare without creating new harm

Verify fasting status using exact time, food or fluid type, and current anesthesia instructions. If the client ate, drank, chewed, smoked, or used a medication outside the plan, report it rather than concealing or automatically cancelling. The anesthesia and procedural teams determine next steps from aspiration risk and urgency.

Implement ordered skin preparation and infection-prevention measures. Do not remove hair routinely; when hair removal is necessary, use the approved clipping method and timing rather than a razor that creates microabrasions. Administer prophylactic antimicrobials at the ordered time and document the dose, route, and completion. Manage glucose, temperature, oxygenation, and colonization precautions according to the client and procedure.

Establish required access, obtain baseline vital signs and targeted tests, empty the bladder when ordered, and apply VTE prophylaxis as prescribed. Secure valuables and label belongings. Teach coughing, deep breathing, incentive-spirometer technique when ordered, splinting, early mobility, pain reporting, leg exercises, equipment, and expected lines or drains. Have the client demonstrate skills before sedation.

Intraoperative nursing protects the whole body

The circulating RN coordinates the room, maintains aseptic and documentation standards, advocates for the unconscious or sedated client, monitors traffic and environment, helps position safely, performs counts with the scrub role, handles specimens, and communicates changes. The scrubbed team maintains the sterile field and manages sterile instruments and supplies. Roles vary by jurisdiction and facility, but accountability is never transferred to the checklist alone.

Protect the sterile field

Inspect packaging, integrity, indicators, expiration, moisture, and sterilization evidence. Treat contamination, uncertainty, or an unobserved field according to policy—do not quietly cover a break. Limit unnecessary traffic, keep doors closed when possible, and communicate any breach immediately so contaminated items can be replaced and exposure evaluated.

Surgical counts occur at required points and include the defined sponges, sharps, instruments, and miscellaneous items. If a count is incorrect, notify the surgeon, repeat and reconcile the count, search systematically, and obtain imaging or follow the retained-item protocol before closure when required. Documentation never substitutes for resolving the discrepancy.

Positioning requires anatomy and time awareness

Maintain alignment, protect pressure points and nerves, secure the client without impairing breathing or circulation, and keep the body within physiologic range. Reassess after table movement, draping, equipment placement, and prolonged time. Supine positioning can injure heels and the ulnar nerve; lithotomy can affect peroneal nerves and hemodynamics; prone positioning requires airway, eye, chest, abdominal, and pressure protection; lateral positioning creates dependent pressure and brachial-plexus risk. Never allow a sedated limb to hang unsupported.

Use safety straps, padding, sequential compression devices, grounding or return electrodes, tourniquets, warming systems, and positioning devices exactly as designed. Document position, devices, skin condition, and reassessment. After surgery, compare neurovascular, skin, vision, and motor findings with baseline.

Fire, energy devices, medications, and specimens

Fire risk rises when an oxidizer, ignition source, and fuel meet. The team assesses risk, manages oxygen concentration and pooling, allows alcohol-based prep to dry, controls drapes and fuels, and communicates before activating electrosurgical, laser, or other ignition sources. Know the local fire-response plan and location of emergency equipment.

Every medication or solution on the sterile field is labeled immediately with name, strength or concentration, and other required information—even if only one product is present. Verbally verify transfers between team members. Handle specimens with two identifiers, exact source and laterality, required medium, and closed-loop read-back; never place a specimen in fixative when fresh, frozen, culture, or other special handling is ordered.

Sign-out completes the operating-room safety loop

Before the client leaves the room, the team confirms the procedure performed, counts, specimen labels, equipment problems, blood loss, and key concerns for recovery. Handoff to PACU includes identity, procedure and site, anesthesia, airway, allergies, medications and last doses, fluids and blood, estimated blood loss, urine, implants, positioning concerns, temperature, pain, drains, dressings, complications, and pending needs.

PACU starts with airway, not pain

On arrival, assess airway patency, respiratory rate and depth, work of breathing, breath sounds, oxygen delivery, saturation trend, circulation, rhythm, blood pressure, perfusion, bleeding, consciousness, neuromuscular recovery, temperature, pain, nausea, dressing, drains, urine, and position. Compare with preoperative baseline and the intraoperative course.

Snoring, paradoxical breathing, obstruction, apnea, slow shallow respirations, rising carbon dioxide, inability to maintain oxygenation, or decreasing consciousness require immediate airway maneuvers, stimulation, oxygenation and ventilation support, reversal or emergency response as ordered. Supplemental oxygen can improve saturation while hypoventilation continues; assess breathing directly.

Oxygen saturation alone can miss hypoventilation
After anesthesia or opioids, evaluate respiratory rate, depth, airway sounds, effort, consciousness, and carbon-dioxide monitoring when used—not only SpO₂.

Hypotension: consider bleeding before reassurance

Evaluate blood-pressure trend with pulse, skin, mental status, capillary refill, dressing and drains, abdominal or operative-site findings, urine output, fluids, blood loss, and medications. A small external stain does not exclude internal hemorrhage. Support circulation, inspect the site, quantify output, maintain access, obtain ordered labs, notify the surgical and anesthesia teams, and escalate rapidly for shock.

Hypertension and tachycardia may reflect pain, hypoxia, hypercarbia, bladder distention, withdrawal, medication effects, or baseline disease. Treat the cause and reassess rather than assuming all postoperative vital-sign changes are pain.

Malignant hyperthermia is a time-critical crisis

Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic reaction to triggering anesthetic agents in susceptible people. Early clues can include an unexpected rapid rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, tachycardia, muscle rigidity, acidosis, hyperkalemia, and increasing temperature; high fever may be a later sign. Stop triggering agents, call for the malignant-hyperthermia cart and emergency support, hyperventilate with high-flow oxygen, and administer dantrolene under the protocol. Begin active cooling when indicated, treat electrolyte and rhythm complications, monitor core temperature, gases, potassium, creatine kinase, coagulation, urine, and kidney function, and prepare for intensive monitoring.

Do not wait for extreme temperature. Document the episode and ensure the client and family receive follow-up information because future anesthesia planning and family evaluation may be needed.

Pain, nausea, temperature, and delirium

Assess pain type, location, intensity, function, sedation, and respiratory status. Sudden pain out of proportion, new chest pain, calf pain, compartment findings, or rapidly increasing surgical-site pain requires evaluation rather than automatic opioid escalation. Use multimodal measures and reassess both relief and adverse effects.

Prevent aspiration by positioning and airway protection while treating postoperative nausea and vomiting. Monitor QT and sedation risks when relevant. Hypothermia can worsen discomfort, coagulation, cardiac stress, and infection risk; use approved warming and reassess. New agitation or confusion may reflect hypoxia, hypercarbia, pain, retention, medication effects, glucose or electrolyte disturbance, stroke, withdrawal, or delirium.

Postoperative complications: recognize the pattern

  • Respiratory: obstruction, hypoventilation, aspiration, atelectasis, pneumonia, bronchospasm, or pulmonary embolism.
  • Circulatory: hemorrhage, shock, myocardial ischemia, dysrhythmia, VTE, or fluid overload.
  • Wound: hematoma, infection, dehiscence, evisceration, ischemia, or drain obstruction.
  • Renal and GI: retention, low urine output, kidney injury, ileus, nausea, constipation, or bowel injury.
  • Neurologic: delayed emergence, delirium, stroke, nerve injury, or residual neuromuscular blockade.

For wound dehiscence or evisceration, stay with the client, call for urgent surgical help, position to reduce tension as tolerated, cover exposed tissue with sterile saline-moistened dressings according to protocol, keep the client NPO, and do not push organs back into the wound.

Prevent complications through recovery

Use lung expansion, upright positioning, coughing, splinting, mobilization, hydration, oral care, and respiratory therapy as appropriate. Apply mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis as ordered and mobilize safely. Maintain aseptic wound and device care, support nutrition and glucose control, remove invasive devices as soon as clinically appropriate, and teach signs of infection or deterioration.

PACU or ambulatory discharge requires more than time elapsed. Apply the facility’s validated criteria to airway, oxygenation, vital signs, consciousness, mobility, pain, nausea, bleeding, intake or voiding when required, and responsible-adult or transportation needs. A score supports judgment but does not override an unstable finding.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify procedure and site, consent, allergies, fasting, medications, comorbidities, baseline airway and function, labs, infection and VTE risks, anesthesia history, and recovery support.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish expected recovery from obstruction, hypoventilation, hemorrhage, shock, malignant hyperthermia, aspiration, VTE, infection, delirium, and wound disruption.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Wrong-person or wrong-site risk before incision and airway compromise, severe bleeding, shock, hypermetabolic crisis, or evisceration after surgery take priority.
  4. Generate solutions: Pause for discrepancies, activate the appropriate checklist or emergency protocol, support ABCs, protect sterility and positioning, and prepare targeted monitoring and rescue resources.
  5. Take action: Advocate before sedation, participate actively in verification and time-out, report breaks and count discrepancies, deliver structured handoff, and intervene rapidly for instability.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess airway, ventilation, circulation, cognition, pain, nausea, temperature, wounds, drains, urine, mobility, infection prevention, understanding, and discharge readiness.

Clinical example

In PACU, a client who received opioids becomes increasingly difficult to arouse, snores, and breathes six shallow breaths per minute while oxygen saturation remains 95% on supplemental oxygen. The RN recognizes hypoventilation despite the saturation, opens and supports the airway, stimulates the client, calls for assistance, supports ventilation, and prepares protocol-directed reversal while continuously reassessing breathing and consciousness. Pain treatment is paused until ventilation is safe.

Original educational synthesis. Perioperative assessment, consent workflow, fasting and medication instructions, antimicrobial timing, skin preparation, roles, counts, positioning, fire prevention, specimen handling, anesthesia rescue, dantrolene use, wound care, monitoring, and discharge require current authorized orders, procedure and anesthesia plans, product instructions, facility policy, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official WHO, CDC, Joint Commission, or NCSBN product.
